PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a United Kingdom national, [ORG] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by [PERSON], lawyers practising in [LOC]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London.

The applicant alleged that the proceedings in which she claimed discrimination at work took an unreasonable length of time contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

On [CODE], the Court declared part of the application inadmissible and adjourned examination of the complaints relating to length of proceedings.

On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. By a decision of [DATETIME], the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible.

The applicant and the Government each filed observations concerning the issue of just satisfaction. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine).

THE FACTS

The applicant, [ORG], is a United Kingdom national, who was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

The applicant commenced employment as a [PERSON] with the [LOC] (“the [PERSON]”) on [CODE]. In [DATETIME], she submitted a formal complaint to the Council's principal Equal Opportunities Officers alleging inter alia harassment and refusal of a promotion on grounds of race. She was interviewed by investigating officers in [DATETIME].

On [CODE], the applicant presented an originating application to the Employment Tribunal alleging that she had been discriminated against as a [PERSON] with a disability, inter alia, due to the decision to give a promotion to another employee instead of herself, the failure to transfer her to another post and the failure to assign her to a higher grade by giving due recognition to her professional qualifications. In her application, she relied on events going back to the commencement of her employment in [DATETIME].

On [DATETIME], one of the Council's investigating officers informed the applicant that her complaints had been found to be unsubstantiated. The applicant sought to appeal the rejection of her complaints pursuant to the Council's internal grievance procedure.

The Employment Tribunal held a hearing on [DATETIME], at which the parties agreed that under section 68(1) of the Race Relations Act 1976, which required that complaints be presented within three [PERSON] of the act complained of, the applicant could not rely upon events taking place before [DATETIME]. Determination of the merits was considered to require detailed evidence and the matter was reserved for a further hearing.

On [DATETIME], the Council made a request for further and better particulars of the originating application. The applicant replied on [DATETIME].

While in the ordinary course of events the hearing on the merits would have been listed for hearing in the [DATETIME], the Council applied to the Employment Tribunal for the merits hearing to be postponed, on the grounds that it would be preferable to await the outcome of the applicant's internal appeal. The matter was adjourned, the applicant making no objection to this adjournment.

The applicant's internal appeal was heard by the Council on [DATETIME]. By letter dated [DATETIME], she was informed that her appeal had been rejected. However, with regard to the applicant's transfer request, the Council committee was concerned at the lack of evidence that any serious consideration was given to this matter and expressed the view that steps should be taken to find the applicant alternative work and to expedite her transfer. Pursuant to this decision, instructions were given to investigate options for a transfer. An offer of transfer was made to the applicant on [DATETIME].

Following the determination of the internal appeal, the Tribunal resumed consideration of the applicant's case, listing the case for a merits hearing on [CODE]. The case lasted longer than anticipated by the parties and it was adjourned and re-listed. The Council had indicated to the Tribunal on [CODE] that it would be possible to reach a negotiated settlement. In the event a settlement was not reached and the Tribunal re-convened on [DATETIME] for a further four [PERSON].

On [DATETIME], the Tribunal issued its decision, finding that there had been discrimination by her employer in a number of procedural aspects.

The proceedings were adjourned for the parties to reach agreement as to the damages payable. The Council had already met with the applicant's trade union representatives on [DATETIME]. Negotiations culminated in a meeting of [DATETIME], in which the Council's legal representatives agreed a settlement figure with the applicant subject to the approval of the elected members of the Council. On [DATETIME], the Council informed the applicant that their members had rejected their officers' recommendations and that no settlement was possible on the terms discussed. The applicant broke off the negotiations entirely the next day.

The Tribunal proposed listing the case in [DATETIME] but as these dates were not convenient for the Council and it appears that the applicant was not available in [DATETIME] the date was fixed for [DATETIME]. After a remedies hearing on that date, the Tribunal made the applicant an award of [QUANTITY]), which decision issued on [DATETIME].

The Council appealed to the Employment Appeal Tribunal (“EAT”). Its notice of appeal had been lodged on [DATETIME], as it was required to be lodged within [DATETIME] of the merits decision.

On [DATETIME], an ex parte preliminary hearing was held by the EAT to determine whether the appeal had reasonable prospects of success. It ordered that the appeal should proceed to a full hearing and required the Employment Tribunal's notes of evidence to be disclosed. These consisted of some 50 [PERSON]. After their transcription, the EAT sent out a listing notice on [DATETIME], giving a hearing date of [CODE].

After the hearing, the EAT delivered judgment on [DATETIME]. It quashed the findings of discrimination.

On [CODE], the applicant filed an application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. Permission was granted by the Court of Appeal on [DATETIME]. The applicant lodged her notice of appeal on [DATETIME]. The bundles of documents were filed on [DATETIME].

After a hearing, on [DATETIME] at which the applicant was represented, the Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's appeal.

The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords on [DATETIME].

On [DATETIME], the applicant sought leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In her petition, she requested exemption under House of Lords Standing Order XIII from the lodgement fee as she was no longer in receipt of legal aid. In [DATETIME], the Appeal Committee of the House of Lords decided to waive the fee. The petition was then formally lodged in [DATETIME]. The applicant supplied the transcripts necessary for the application on [CODE]. The House of Lords refused leave on [DATETIME].

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [CODE]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by [PERSON], lawyers practising in [LOC] (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions.

The applicant alleged under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that he had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the [ORG] which tried and convicted him. He further complained under Article 6 § 3 (b) that the written opinion of the chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation had never been served on him, thus depriving him of the opportunity to put forward his counter-arguments. He finally contended that he had been convicted merely on account of his association with a left-wing magazine, in violation of his rights under Articles 9 and 10.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATETIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1).

By a decision of [DATETIME] the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal and his right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).

On [DATETIME] the case was assigned to the Third Section of the Court.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

On [DATETIME] the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody by police officers from the [ORG]. He was accused of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, the [ORG]).

On [DATETIME] the public prosecutor attached to the [ORG] filed an indictment with the latter charging the applicant, under Articles 168 § 2 and 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act, with membership of an illegal organisation.

On [DATETIME] found the applicant guilty of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, the [ORG], and sentenced him to [DATETIME] imprisonment and debarred him from public service for [DATETIME].

The applicant appealed. On [DATETIME] the chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion (tebliğname) on the merits of the appeal to the Court of Cassation. The chief public prosecutor proposed that the first instance court’s judgment be upheld. The written opinion of the chief public prosecutor was read out during the hearing before the Court of Cassation.

On [DATETIME] the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal upholding the [ORG] judgment.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [CODE].

The [DEM] Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON], of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATETIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

On [DATETIME] the Fourth Section decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

On [DATETIME] the applicant filed with the [ORG]) a petition in which he requested the annulment of a judgment delivered in [DATETIME] in criminal proceedings against him, submitting that they had been of a political nature. He also claimed compensation.

On [DATETIME] the court annulled that judgment. However, its decision did not relate to the compensation claim.

On [DATETIME] the applicant filed another compensation claim.

Subsequently, he lodged several complaints concerning the inactivity of the court, but to no avail.

In her letters of [DATETIME], in reply to the applicant's complaints, a judge of the Regional Court informed the applicant that the delay in the examination of his compensation claim was caused by a large number of similar requests lodged with that court and the dearth of judges.

On [CODE] the court held a hearing. A public prosecutor requested that the proceedings be stayed, submitting that a part of the Regional Court's decision of [DATETIME] was invalid and required supplementation. Subsequently, the court stayed the proceedings.

The hearing scheduled for [DATETIME] was adjourned at the applicant's request.

On [DATETIME] the Regional Court asked the [ORG] (Ur[PERSON]) to submit certain documents. The documents were submitted to the court on [DATETIME].

On [DATETIME] the proceedings were resumed.

The court adjourned the hearing scheduled for [DATETIME], as the proceedings concerning the annulment of the criminal judgment against the applicant given in [DATETIME] had not been completed.

On [DATETIME] gave judgment. It awarded the applicant [ORG] in compensation. He did not lodge an appeal against that judgment.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [CODE]/[CODE]) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by [PERSON] (“the applicant”) on [CODE].

The applicant was unrepresented. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London.

The applicant complained that the United Kingdom authorities’ refusal to grant him Widow’s Bereavement Allowance or equivalent constituted discrimination on grounds of sex contrary to Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No.[CODE].

By a partial decision of [DATETIME] the Court decided to communicate this application. It also decided to join this application to other applications (nos.[PERSON]/00, 60933/00, 60937/00, 60944/00, 61038/00, 61388/00, 61949/00, 62776/00 63388/00, 63464/00, 63469/00, 63470/00, 63473/00, 63474/00, 63584/00, 63645/00, 63701/00, 63702/00 and[DATETIME]).

On [CODE], after obtaining the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible in so far as the complaint concerned Widow’s Bereavement Allowance and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

His wife died on [DATETIME]. On [DATETIME] the applicant made a claim to the Inland Revenue requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow, namely Widow’s Bereavement Allowance (“WBA”), for the years [DATETIME]/99 an[DATETIME]. On [CODE] the Inland Revenue informed him that he was ineligible for WBA as he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The applicant was represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOC]. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador [PERSON], Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs.

On [CODE] the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3).

The German Government did not make use of their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention).

THE FACTS

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant is a [PERSON] who was appointed at [ORG]. Under the terms of appointment he was entitled to reimbursement of the removal costs and to a household allowance. In [DATETIME] the sum of [QUANTITY]) was paid to the applicant.

On [DATETIME] the applicant claimed reimbursement of the remaining removal costs in the sum of [ORG] and payment of the household allowance in the sum of [ORG], plus [QUANTITY] interest since [DATETIME].

The [ORG] dismissed the applicant’s claim on [DATETIME].

The applicant appealed on [DATETIME] to the Ministry of Education, Science and Culture (“the Ministry”).

The Ministry did not decide within the statutory six-month time-limit laid down in section 73 § 1 of the General Administrative Proceedings Act. In [DATETIME] the applicant brought court proceedings relating to the claims at issue. A conditional settlement was reached but was revoked by the applicant in [DATETIME]. The applicant’s action was dismissed in [DATETIME].

Meanwhile, on [DATETIME], the applicant complained to the Administrative Court under Article 132 of the Federal Constitution about the administration’s failure to determine his claim. On [CODE] the Administrative Court ordered the Ministry of Education to issue a decision within [DATETIME].

On [DATETIME] the Ministry dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court on [DATETIME]. The Ministry filed observations in reply on [DATETIME].

On [DATETIME] the Administrative Court quashed the Ministry’s decision as being unlawful.

By decision of [DATETIME] the Ministry referred the case back to the [ORG] for a new decision. Meanwhile on [DATETIME] the applicant supplemented his claims, apparently requesting reimbursement of costs incurred for travelling between [LOC] and his former place of residence.

On [DATETIME] the applicant was summoned to a hearing and two [DATETIME] the sum of [ORG] was paid to the applicant with a view to reaching a settlement.

The hearing took place on [DATETIME]. According to the minutes the hearing served the purpose of establishing the plausibility of the applicant’s claims as submitted on [DATETIME] and supplemented on [DATETIME] and to determine their amount with the participation of the applicant. It is then noted that, in the light of the explanations given, the costs and interest claimed seemed plausible. At the close of the hearing the parties concluded a friendly settlement with the following terms: “(a) [ORG] thus declares its willingness to transfer, in addition to the payment already made of [ORG] and the regulated transport costs in the amount of [ORG], the lump-sum of [DATETIME] to the account of [PERSON]. (b) [PERSON], for his part, withdraws all requests in connection with the proceedings at issue. As a result, the demands and claims asserted in the present proceedings are completely settled and complied with.”

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [CODE]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The [DEM] (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention.

On [DATETIME] the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [PERSON] and lives in [DEM].

In [DATETIME] the applicant donated his agricultural property to his son.[DATETIME] the public notary prepared an amendment to the contract concerning the transfer of certain items of property (agricultural equipment) to the applicant's son.[DATETIME]) confirmed that the amendment was invalid.

On [DATETIME] the applicant sued his son, [CODE]., before the [ORG]) for restitution of the items of property in question. The applicant indicated that the value of the claim was [QUANTITY]). He also asked to be exempted from court fees.

On [DATETIME] the Regional Court refused to exempt the applicant from court fees. The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The applicant submitted that his only income was a disability pension in the amount of [ORG]]. He further claimed that he did not own any real estate or any other assets, except for a car. However, he had been paying for it in instalments: [CODE]. The plaintiff estimated the amount of his monthly expenses for his flat at [ORG]]. From the documents submitted by the applicant it appears that the sum he spends monthly on his flat, and the loan for the car customised for a disabled person, amounts to [ORG]. After he pays for the flat and the loan, the plaintiff has [ORG]]. According to the court, it is not enough to cover his maintenance costs such as food, clothes and medication... This leads the court to the conclusion that the plaintiff has other additional resources and he can afford to pay the court fees in question. Consequently, considering that the plaintiff failed to indicate all his assets, the court dismisses his application for an exemption from court fees.”

On [DATETIME] the applicant filed an interlocutory appeal against this decision. He also filed a new motion for an exemption from court fees.

The [ORG] rejected the applicant's interlocutory appeal as it had been lodged outside the prescribed time-limit. On [DATETIME] upheld this decision.

On [DATETIME] the Regional Court ordered the applicant to supplement his motion for an exemption from court fees.

In reply the applicant stressed that his financial situation had not changed and was still very bad. His disability benefit had increased by [ORG], as shown by a pay slip he had attached.

On [DATETIME] rejected the applicant's second motion for exemption from court fees. The court held that it had already considered the applicant's financial situation and found that it had not justified an exemption.

The applicant filed an interlocutory appeal. He submitted that he was [DATETIME] and in poor health. He was not even able to buy the necessary medication as his monthly disability pension amounted to [ORG]. For these reasons he believed that he should be exempted from court fees.

On [DATETIME] dismissed the applicant's interlocutory appeal against this decision. The court repeated the reasons given by the Regional Court.

On [CODE] the Regional Court ordered the applicant to pay [ORG]] for lodging his statement of claim on pain of having it returned.

As the applicant failed to do so, his statement of claim was returned to him on [DATETIME].

PROCEDURE

The case originated in two applications (nos. [DATETIME]/95 [DATETIME]) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON], (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The [DEM] (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that his correspondence with the Convention organs was, while he was detained on remand, twice intercepted, opened and read by the prison authorities and by the court before which the criminal proceedings against him were pending.

The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On [DATETIME] the Court decided to join the applications.

On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section.

By a decision of [DATETIME] the Court declared the applications partly admissible.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant is a [DEM] national, who was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

Two letters from the Secretariat of the European Commission of Human Rights, posted on [DATETIME] and on [DATETIME], were intercepted, opened and read by the administration of the [ORG], where the applicant was detained on remand. They were subsequently forwarded to the [LOC], before which criminal proceedings against the applicant were pending at that time, and were read by the court.

On [DATETIME] the applicant requested the President of the [LOC] to explain what was the legal basis on which his correspondence with the European Commission of Human Rights had been opened and read.

He reiterated his complaint on [DATETIME] in a letter to the President of the Regional Court. In reply, on [DATETIME] the President of the Regional Court informed him that Article 8 of the Convention did not prohibit censorship of correspondence of persons detained on remand. It was also permitted under Section 33 § 2 of the Rules of Detention on Remand. The correspondence sent to the European Commission of Human Rights fell within the scope of this provision. It was further stated that the text of the Convention did not contain provisions relating to the inviolability of the correspondence to and from the European Commission of Human Rights.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[PERSON]) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a British national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The applicant was represented by [PERSON], solicitors in [LOC]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows.

On [CODE] the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

His wife died on [CODE] leaving dependent children. His second claim for widows’ benefits was made in [DATETIME] and was rejected on [DATETIME] on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. On [DATETIME] the applicant applied for reconsideration and on [CODE] he was requested to complete another claim form. The applicant did so and his claim was rejected on [DATETIME]. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

At the time of his claim the applicant was in receipt of child benefit.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, [ORG] (“the applicant”), on [CODE].

The applicant was represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [PERSON]. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent.

On [CODE] the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [PERSON].

On [DATETIME] the applicant was admitted to the military service.

On [DATETIME] he went to see a doctor at the [ORG] for an eye[CODE]. His medical report stated that he had [CODE] reduced [CODE]) on his left [PERSON]. The report noted that the applicant had complained that he had had the problem on his left [PERSON] since childhood. Accordingly, the applicant was discharged from the military as he was no longer eligible for service.

On [DATETIME], the applicant applied to both, the Retired Civil Servant’s Fund for a pension and to the Compensation Commission at the Ministry of the Interior for compensation. Both requests were rejected.

On [DATETIME] the applicant obtained a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtarlık) attesting his indigence.

On [DATETIME], the applicant brought an action against the Ministry of the Interior before the Supreme Military Administrative Court requesting compensation of [ORG]. In his petition the applicant alleged, inter alia, that he had no such eye problems prior to his service in the army. He further referred to the doctrine of “social risk”, which did not require the establishment of any causal link between the harmful action and the loss. The applicant also requested legal aid to cover the payment of the court fees.

On [DATETIME] the Supreme Military Administrative Court, after examining the case file and hearing the observations of the rapporteur, dismissed the applicant’s request for legal aid on the ground that the case was not well‑founded.

On [DATETIME], the Supreme Military Administrative Court notified the applicant that he was required to pay a court fee which was [ORG]).

In the meantime, on [DATETIME], the applicant was examined by doctors at [ORG]. The latter confirmed that the applicant had [CODE] amounting to [QUANTITY].

On [CODE], the court discontinued the proceedings on the ground that the applicant failed to pay the necessary court fees.

On [DATETIME] the applicant was notified of this decision.

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATETIME].

The applicant was represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOC]. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent.

On [CODE] the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3).

THE FACTS

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [LOC].

On [DATETIME] the applicant, who worked in a private company at the material time, had an accident during working hours that led to his [PERSON].

On [DATETIME] the applicant lodged an action with the [ORG] against his employer, requesting compensation for the pecuniary damage he had suffered as a result of the accident.

On [DATETIME] the applicant lodged another action with the same court against his employer, this time requesting compensation for non‑pecuniary damage.

On [DATETIME] the court joined two cases.

During the proceedings the first-instance court postponed the hearings awaiting information and documents from a number of State authorities, such as the public prosecutor's office and the Social Security Institution, as well as the reports of experts appointed by the court.

On [DATETIME] partially accepted the applicant's claims and awarded him compensation for non-pecuniary damage, plus interest at the statutory rate, running from the date of the incident.

On [CODE] the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first instance court.

In his submissions of [DATETIME], the applicant informed the Court that he had filed a case with the [ORG] against the company, requesting additional compensation (munzam zarar) for the damage he had sustained as a result of the delay in payment. This case was dismissed on [DATETIME].

In his letter of [DATETIME] to the Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that the courts' refusal to grant him additional compensation violated his right to property.

The applicant's complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention was separated from the present application and was registered under application no. [CODE]/[CODE].

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. [DATETIME]/[CODE]) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged on [DATETIME] with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [DEM] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”).

The British Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON], of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATETIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

On [CODE] the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.

THE FACTS

The applicant was born in [DATETIME] and lives in [PERSON].

On [DATETIME] powder (subsequently found to be starch) were found in the belly tank of the apparently unladen lorry which the applicant had just brought into the United [LOC]. The applicant was arrested, and on [DATETIME] he was charged with knowingly being involved in the attempted import of a controlled drug ([PERSON]). He was convicted on [DATETIME] and sentenced to [DATETIME]’ imprisonment. His application for leave to appeal arrived at the Criminal Appeals Office on [DATETIME], and leave to appeal and legal aid were granted on [DATETIME].

The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on [DATETIME]. As to sentence it found as follows: “76. ... The points ... are, first, that no [PERSON] was imported and that seems to us to be the most important point, namely that this was an offence of attempt and not of actual importation.

Second, that the appellant appears to have occupied a lowly position in what was undoubtedly an extensive chain, stretching from source abroad into this country.

Further, it awarded the applicant sole custody over the couple’s daughter and ordered that she should reside with him in case of her return.

On [DATETIME] the applicant filed a request for recognition of the divorce decree with the Austrian Federal Ministry of Justice.

On [CODE] the Federal Ministry of Justice refused to grant this request. Referring to Section 24 § 1 of the Fourth Implementing Regulation to the Marriage Act (4. Durchführungsverordnung zum Ehegesetz), it considered that a recognition of the divorce decree would be contrary to Austrian ordre public as the applicant’s wife, being the defendant in the proceedings before the [ORG], had not been heard as she was considered to be in default, despite the fact that the applicant’s petition for divorce had not been duly served on her.

It argued that Article 6 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms which has constitutional rank in Austrian law, applied to the proceedings concerning the recognition of foreign divorce decrees as their outcome had a direct effect on the civil law relationship of the persons concerned. However, it was incompatible with that Article that the Federal Ministry of Justice, an administrative authority, decided upon the request for recognition. The subsequent control by the Administrative Court was not sufficient where the subject matter, such as family law relations, fell within the very core of the notion of “civil rights”.

The Constitutional Court received the Administrative Court’s request on [DATETIME]. The Administrative Court submitted three further requests raising the same issue, which were received by the Constitutional Court on [DATETIME], respectively. The proceedings in these cases were joined to proceedings in the applicant’s case.

On [DATETIME] it supplemented its requests in the three other cases.

On [DATETIME] the Constitutional Court gave its judgment, finding that Section 24 § 1 of the Fourth Implementing Regulation to the Marriage Act was in conformity with the constitution.

The Constitutional Court noted firstly that the proceedings at issue were concerned with the questions whether recognition was compatible with Austrian ordre public. Thus, the recognition of foreign divorce decrees was closely linked to the question whether they could be enforced in Austria. Referring to a number of decisions, in which the European Commission of Human Rights had found that Article 6 did not apply to enforcement proceedings, the Constitutional Court expressed doubts as to the applicability of Article 6.

Even assuming that Article 6 applied, referring to the Court’s Zumtobel v. Austria judgment (of [DATETIME], Series A no. 268-A), the Constitutional Court held that the Administrative Court’s scope of review was sufficient, since proceedings concerning the recognition of foreign divorce decrees involved mainly questions of law. Where an assessment of facts was required, as for instance where the question arose whether an action had been duly served, the Administrative Court was empowered to review whether the administrative authority’s assessment was correctly based on the contents of the file.

On [DATETIME] having resumed its proceedings, the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The decision was served on the applicant on [DATETIME].

Another trade union, [ORG], and a number of employees also made representations to [ORG] about the applicant’s continued employment.

After taking legal advice [ORG] summarily dismissed him on [DATETIME] cited, inter alia, potential health and safety risks as the applicant’s continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. It also expressed concern that the applicant’s continued employment could jeopardise its reputation and possibly lead to the loss of its contract with [ORG].

The applicant therefore lacked sufficient continuous service to bring an action for unfair dismissal. However, on [CODE] he lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act 1976 (“the 1976 Act”).

The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. The racial grounds relied on were those of the passengers and employees of [ORG] who were of [DEM]. He further argued that since the [ORG] was a “wh[PERSON]-only” party, his dismissal also constituted indirect racial discrimination.

The Employment Tribunal gave judgment on [DATETIME]. It noted [ORG]’s concerns that the applicant’s continued employment might lead to difficulties with other employees; damage its relationship with the unions; lead to attacks on [ORG]’s minibuses which would jeopardise the health and safety of [ORG]’s staff, its vulnerable passengers, and the applicant himself; cause considerable anxiety amongst [ORG]’s passengers and those relatives/carers entrusting vulnerable passengers to its care; and damage its reputation so as potentially to place at risk existing contracts and future bids for work in the public sector and elsewhere.

The Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The Tribunal also dismissed the claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, namely the maintenance of health and safety.

The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On [DATETIME] his appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase “on racial grounds” by failing to interpret its meaning broadly and had not indicated how it had come to the conclusion that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving the aim of ensuring health and safety because, inter alia, there had been no consideration of any alternatives to dismissal.

On [CODE] the Court of Appeal allowed [ORG]’s appeal and restored the order of the Employment Tribunal. [PERSON] found the applicant’s submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation.

In rejecting the claim of direct discrimination, the Court of Appeal noted that: “[PERSON] was treated less favourably not on the ground that he was white, but on the ground of a particular non-racial characteristic shared by him with a tiny proportion of the white population, that is membership of and standing for election for a political party like the [LOC] was not adopting a policy which discriminated on the basis of a dividing line of colour or race. [ORG] would apply the same approach to a member of a similar political party, which confined its membership to [PERSON] people. The dividing line of colour or race was not made by [ORG], but by the [ORG] which defines its own composition by colour or race. [PERSON] cannot credibly make a claim of direct race discrimination by [ORG] against him on the ground that he is white by relying on the decision of his own chosen political party to limit its membership to white people. The [ORG] cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Properly analysed [PERSON]’s complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws.”

In rejecting the claim of indirect discrimination, the following was noted: “For indirect discrimination ... it is necessary to identify a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ which [ORG] has applied or would apply equally to persons not of the same race or colour. ... [PERSON] ... failed to present the tribunal with a case, which satisfied the requisite elements of a claim for indirect race discrimination and upon which the tribunal could properly make a finding of indirect race discrimination.... However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the [ORG]) to be meaningful. A provision of ‘membership of the [ORG]’ could not be applied to a person who was not of the same colour as [PERSON], because only persons of the same colour as him ([PERSON]) are eligible to be members of the [ORG]. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation like the [ORG], which existed to promote views hostile to members of a different colour than those that belonged to the organisation. If such a provision were applied, however, it would not put persons of the same race as [PERSON] ‘at a particular disadvantage’ when compared with other persons within section 1(1A) of the 1976 Act. All such political activists would be at the same disadvantage, whatever colour they were.”

Lastly, with regard to the applicant’s contention that he had been subjected to less favourable treatment arising from membership of a political party contrary to his Convention rights under Articles 9, 10, 11 and 14 and that this should have been taken into account in deciding whether indirect discrimination had been justified, the Court of Appeal stated that: “The [DATETIME] Act does not assist [PERSON] in this case. He is not entitled to make a claim under it as [ORG] is not a public authority. Section 3 of the 1998 Act does not assist, as there is no respect in which the relevant provisions of the 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights. As for justification under the 1976 Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirect discrimination has been made out.”

The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords.
